items.name: Geist + Inter
items.vibe: The default voice of a well-built developer product — rational, unfussy, and confident enough not to decorate.
items.pairing: Both are neutral grotesques with near-identical proportions, so the handoff is invisible — but Geist's tighter spacing and more rational, closed apertures give it a deliberate edge at 48px where Inter reads generic, while Inter's taller x-height and open apertures keep 14–16px UI text more legible than Geist manages.
items.notes: Deliberately low-contrast: if the headline needs to *announce*, this isn't it — reach for Space Grotesk or Bricolage Grotesque. Geist and Geist Mono share metrics, so code blocks lock to the same vertical rhythm. Both run 100–900; stop at 700, the 800/900 cuts fill in at UI sizes.

items.name: Space Grotesk + Inter
items.vibe: Engineered but not sterile — a product that ships fast and has opinions about its own typography.
items.pairing: Space Grotesk is a proportional redraw of Space Mono, so it smuggles monospace quirks — the flattened curves, the odd angled terminals — into headlines, which is the entire personality. Inter has none of that, and that is exactly why it belongs in body copy: it gets out of the way. Their x-heights are close enough that a hero and the paragraph under it read as one system.
items.notes: Space Grotesk tops out at 700 and has no italic — plan emphasis around weight and size. It thins out badly below 14px; never use it for body copy or table labels.

items.name: JetBrains Mono + IBM Plex Sans
items.vibe: Headlines set in code — for a tool unapologetically aimed at people who read monospace all day.
items.pairing: Setting the headline in the same mono as the code samples is the signal: this is a tool, not a brand. It only works because IBM Plex Sans underneath is a genuinely neutral humanist sans with normal proportions — it absorbs the paragraph load that JetBrains Mono's fixed advance width would make exhausting after two lines.
items.css: --font-display: 'JetBrains Mono', monospace; --font-body: 'IBM Plex Sans', sans-serif; --font-mono: 'JetBrains Mono', monospace;
items.notes: Keep mono headlines under ~40 characters and never center them — the fixed advance width makes ragged centering look like a bug. JetBrains Mono has a deliberately tall x-height, so it sets visually larger than a sans at the same px; drop the headline 1–2px. Plex Sans carries a wdth axis (75–100) if you need a condensed cut for dense docs nav.

items.name: IBM Plex Serif + IBM Plex Sans
items.vibe: Institutional, audited, and calm — the typography of a company that holds your money and wants you to know it's boring.
items.pairing: One superfamily, three jobs. Plex Serif and Plex Sans share a skeleton and metrics, so the serif reads as "institution" without introducing a second personality that a compliance-heavy page cannot afford — and Plex Mono, drawn to the same rhythm, gives balances and account numbers a fixed advance width so columns of money line up and stop jittering on refresh.
items.css: --font-display: 'IBM Plex Serif', serif; --font-body: 'IBM Plex Sans', sans-serif; --font-mono: 'IBM Plex Mono', monospace;
items.notes: Plex Serif and Plex Mono are static-only on Google Fonts (no variable axes) — every weight is a separate file, and three families is already a heavy download, so request only the weights listed here. Set every figure in Plex Mono, not the sans. Plex tops out at 700; there is no black.

items.name: Fraunces + Source Serif 4
items.vibe: An old soul with a modern printing press — warm, slightly strange, and built for people who actually read.
items.pairing: Fraunces is a display serif with a WONK axis and a 9–144 optical-size range — at 72px its wonky, off-kilter details and heavy contrast give a masthead genuine character. Source Serif 4 has no such ambition, and that is the point: it holds an even, quiet color down a 2,000-word column where Fraunces would strobe. Both sit on the same old-style stress, so the page reads as one voice at two volumes.
items.notes: Fraunces is variable with opsz 9–144 — pin it high for headings (`font-variation-settings: 'opsz' 96`) or set `font-optical-sizing: auto`, otherwise you get text-optimised shapes that look weak at display size. Never use Fraunces for body: its contrast shreds below 18px. Source Serif 4 starts at 200 but 400 is the body weight — 300 is too light on white.

items.name: Cormorant Garamond + Jost
items.vibe: Quiet money — hairline display serif over a geometric sans that refuses to raise its voice.
items.pairing: Cormorant Garamond is a Garamond revival drawn deliberately for display — fine hairlines, small x-height, generous ascenders — which reads as heritage. Jost is a Futura-derived geometric with a large x-height and zero historical baggage. The tension between a 16th-century serif and a 20th-century geometric is the modern-luxury move, and Jost's neutrality is what keeps it from turning into costume drama.
items.notes: Cormorant Garamond's small x-height makes it set visually smaller than its px value — size headings up 10–15% against a grotesque. It runs 300–700 only. Use Jost 400 for body; its 300 disappears on white and will fail AA. Jost wants generous tracking (0.08em+) when you use it for small-caps nav.

items.name: Playfair Display + Source Sans 3
items.vibe: Composed and literate — high-contrast elegance that still behaves itself on a settings page.
items.pairing: Playfair's Didone-adjacent thick/thin contrast and strong vertical stress need a body face offering the opposite — Source Sans 3 is near-monolinear with open apertures, drawn by Adobe explicitly for UI legibility, so it never competes for the eye. They share the same upright vertical axis, which is why the page doesn't feel like two unrelated fonts stapled together.
items.notes: Playfair Display starts at 400 — there is no light weight, so don't design a hairline hero around it. Its hairlines break up below ~24px; keep it to h1/h2. Honest warning: this pairing is well-travelled to the point of cliché — if the brief is "we need to look different", it will not do that for you.

items.name: Bodoni Moda + Karla
items.vibe: Cover-of-Vogue energy — extreme contrast, acres of white space, and absolute confidence.
items.pairing: Bodoni Moda is a true Didone — the hairlines are the entire point and they only survive at display size, where they read as fashion masthead. Karla is a low-contrast grotesque with slightly odd, tightly-drawn letterforms: enough personality to not feel like a default, but an even enough color to hand all the drama to the Bodoni. That is the correct division of labour.
items.notes: Bodoni Moda has an opsz axis (6–96) — pin it to ~96 for a hero or use `font-optical-sizing: auto`; at the text-optimised default the hairlines are thickened and the whole reason you chose it disappears. Never set it below 28px. Weights start at 400 — there is no light cut. Karla runs 200–800.

items.name: Fredoka + Nunito
items.vibe: Round, bouncy, and safe for small hands — nothing here has a sharp corner.
items.pairing: Both are rounded-terminal faces so the family feeling is instant — but Fredoka is a chunky, wide, almost inflated display with tiny apertures that would be unreadable in a paragraph, while Nunito is a rounded sans with normal proportions and a tall x-height that a seven-year-old (or a parent at 11pm) can actually read. Same warmth, two very different jobs.
items.notes: Fredoka runs 300–700 with a wdth axis (75–125) and no italic; it is display-only — anything under 20px turns to mush. Nunito goes to 1000 but 700 is plenty for kid-facing UI. For early readers, push line-height to 1.6+ and avoid all-caps entirely — caps strip the word-shape cues new readers rely on.

items.name: Outfit + Figtree
items.vibe: Approachable modern consumer — the friendly end of geometric, without tipping into cute.
items.pairing: Outfit is a strict geometric — near-perfect circles, single-storey shapes — which looks sharp in a headline but goes monotonous in a paragraph because every letter is the same shape and the eye has nothing to grab. Figtree keeps the geometric warmth but restores humanist details and a taller x-height, so body copy reads at speed. A geometric brand with a readable interior.
items.notes: Outfit has no italic at all — emphasis in a heading has to come from weight. All the flexibility lives in the body face: Figtree covers 300–900 with true italics. Outfit's tight apertures make it a poor choice below 16px, so keep it out of labels and captions.

items.name: Archivo Black + Archivo
items.vibe: Loud, flat, and undesigned on purpose — type as a blunt instrument.
items.pairing: Same skeleton, maximum mass — the jump from a screaming headline to body copy is pure weight with zero change in personality, and that flatness is precisely the brutalist move: nothing has been styled, one typeface is simply shouting. Space Mono's mechanical, quirky digits then supply the raw "system output" texture the style lives on.
items.notes: Archivo Black is a separately drawn single 400 weight with no italic — it is not "Archivo at 900", and you must never `font-weight: bold` it; the browser will synthesise a smeared fake. Archivo itself is variable with a wdth axis (62–125) if you want a condensed cut. Set Archivo Black tight (letter-spacing: -0.02em) at display size; it's drawn loose for print.

items.name: Space Mono + IBM Plex Mono
items.vibe: Everything is monospaced and that is the entire aesthetic — terminal green optional.
items.pairing: The point is that nothing escapes the grid, so the pairing is really a division of character: Space Mono's exaggerated, almost slab-serifed quirks carry the headline personality, while IBM Plex Mono is the rare mono with seven weights and a genuinely drawn italic — enough range to survive as actual body copy, which almost no other monospace manages.
items.css: --font-display: 'Space Mono', monospace; --font-body: 'IBM Plex Mono', monospace; --font-mono: 'IBM Plex Mono', monospace;
items.notes: Monospace body copy costs ~40% more horizontal space and measurable reading speed — cap the measure at ~60ch and don't do this on a page anyone has to read carefully. Space Mono has only 400/700. If the design needs to be legible more than it needs to be a mood, use `jetbrains-mono-ibm-plex-sans` instead.

items.name: Poppins + DM Sans
items.vibe: Clean geometric modernism — circles, straight lines, and nothing to apologise for.
items.pairing: Poppins is a pure monolinear geometric with single-storey letterforms — gorgeous at 48px, exhausting at 16px because the circles give the eye no distinguishing features. DM Sans keeps the geometric skeleton but restores a double-storey "a" and shortens the descenders, so the body stays fast to read while the family voice holds. Same genre, different jobs — which is why it doesn't read as two brands.
items.notes: Poppins has near-identical ascender and x-height, so it looks larger than its px value — set it 1–2px smaller than instinct says. It is static-only (no variable axis): every weight is a separate file, so never request all nine. DM Sans's opsz axis (9–40) handles small-size spacing for you.

items.name: Alegreya + Alegreya Sans
items.vibe: Warm, literate, and slightly irregular — a well-set book that isn't trying to be neutral.
items.pairing: Huerta Tipográfica drew these as a matched superfamily, so rhythm and proportion already agree exactly. The contrast is temperature, not shape: Alegreya's calligraphic origin gives headings a deliberate irregularity — asymmetric serifs, a stress that wobbles — that reads as a human hand, while Alegreya Sans keeps that humanist skeleton with the serifs removed, so the body is calm without going cold.
items.notes: Trap: Alegreya Sans has an irregular weight set — 100, 300, 400, 500, 700, 800, 900. There is no 200 and no 600, and requesting one returns HTTP 400 from Google Fonts and silently kills the whole stylesheet. Alegreya starts at 400 (no light). Both ship true italics, which is rare and worth using in longform.

items.name: Anton + Barlow
items.vibe: Stadium volume — ultra-condensed caps that hit like a scoreboard.
items.pairing: Anton is a single-weight ultra-condensed grotesque built for exactly one job — filling a headline edge-to-edge with maximum ink. Barlow is a low-contrast grotesque drawn in the same slightly-condensed, signage-derived idiom, so body copy under a huge Anton headline reads as the same brand rather than a fallback. The contrast here is scale and density, not style.
items.notes: Anton is 400-only with no italic and no lighter cut — it is a display face, full stop; nothing below 32px. Its default fit is very tight; that's intended, don't "fix" it. Barlow is static-only across 100–900 plus italics, so request only the weights you use.

items.name: Libre Franklin + Lora
items.vibe: A newspaper that moved online without losing its spine — authoritative, dense, readable.
items.pairing: Libre Franklin is an open revival of Franklin Gothic — the American newspaper headline face for most of a century — which is precisely the authority a headline gets to borrow. Lora underneath is a brushed serif with moderate contrast that holds an even color through a 2,000-word scroll where a high-contrast Didone would strobe. Sans headline over serif body is the actual newspaper convention, not a pastiche of one.
items.notes: Lora runs 400–700 only — no light, no black; build hierarchy with size, not weight. Set Lora body at 18–19px: it has a moderate x-height and gets tiring at 16. Libre Franklin is variable 100–900, so its weight range is effectively free.

items.name: Public Sans + EB Garamond
items.vibe: Scholarly and unshowy — the argument matters, the typography gets out of its way.
items.pairing: This inverts the usual order on purpose. Public Sans — the US government's neutral grotesque — makes headings, figure captions and running heads read as *apparatus*: structural furniture you navigate by rather than voice. That frees EB Garamond, a faithful Claude Garamont revival, to carry the actual argument with the long-form comfort a 6,000-word paper demands.
items.notes: EB Garamond runs 400–800 with italics — the italic is excellent and is the right tool for Latin terms and cited titles. Its x-height is small, so set body at 19–20px, not 16. Keep Public Sans at 600/700 and let EB Garamond stay the largest thing on the page; if the sans starts competing, the hierarchy has inverted.

items.name: Newsreader + Mulish
items.vibe: Clinical without being cold — a healthcare product that sounds like a person, not a form.
items.pairing: A serif in healthcare is a deliberate de-clinicalising move — Newsreader's low contrast and soft, bookish serifs make a heading read as a person talking to you rather than a hospital form. Mulish underneath is a minimalist sans with rounded terminals and a tall x-height drawn for screens, so dosage instructions and consent copy stay legible on a phone held at arm's length. Warmth on top, clarity where it's load-bearing.
items.notes: Newsreader has an opsz axis (6–72) — set `font-optical-sizing: auto` so headings pick up the display cut. Keep weights moderate (500/600); heavy serifs in a medical context read as alarming. Mulish goes to 1000, but anything above 700 undoes the calm. The type is the small lever here: this audience skews older, so contrast ratios and target sizes matter more than the font choice.

items.name: DM Serif Display + Nunito Sans
items.vibe: Appetite in type — a chalkboard menu that had a very good art director.
items.pairing: DM Serif Display has high contrast and generous ball terminals that read as hand-lettered signage at 40px+ — warm and a little indulgent, exactly what a menu wants — but it is a display cut and collapses below 24px. Nunito Sans does the unglamorous half: rounded terminals keep the warmth, while a tall x-height and a text-tuned opsz axis keep an ingredient list or an allergen warning readable at 14px.
items.notes: DM Serif Display ships exactly one weight (400) plus a true italic — there is no bold, so hierarchy must come from size and colour and never from `font-weight`. The italic is genuinely lovely; use it for dish names. Nunito Sans's opsz axis maxes at 12 — it is tuned for text, so build sub-heads from size, not from this face's display ambitions.

items.name: Marcellus + Raleway
items.vibe: Somewhere old and worth the flight — inscriptional capitals over air and horizon.
items.pairing: Marcellus is drawn from Roman inscriptional capitals — it reads as something carved: a monument, a passport stamp. That register is what travel is selling and no geometric sans can fake it. Raleway's high x-height and usable light weights then sit quietly over full-bleed photography without fighting it, and its slightly narrow, elegant proportions sustain the tone Marcellus sets.
items.notes: Marcellus is a single 400 weight with no italic and no bold — never synthesise one; the browser's fake bold destroys the inscriptional shapes. Size it up instead. It's strongest in Title Case or ALL CAPS with 0.05em+ tracking. Raleway 300 works over dark photography but fails AA on white — switch to 400 for body on light backgrounds.

items.name: Chakra Petch + Rubik
items.vibe: HUD energy — clipped corners, angular terminals, and a scoreboard that never sleeps.
items.pairing: Chakra Petch's clipped corners and squared-off terminals are pure HUD — perfect for a headline or a stat, punishing for anything longer than a line. Rubik shares that squarish skeleton but rounds the corners instead of cutting them, so patch notes and menus stay readable while still reading as the same hardware. Space Mono takes timers and scores, where a fixed advance width stops digits jumping between frames.
items.notes: Chakra Petch runs 300–700 with a true oblique italic that looks right on a leaderboard. Don't set it below 16px — the clipped corners fill in and it just looks blurry. Rubik covers 300–900. If the game skews sci-fi rather than competitive, swap the display for Syne.

items.name: Syne + DM Sans
items.vibe: Engineered but faintly alien — a research lab that also ships a product and hasn't decided which it is.
items.pairing: Syne's widths are deliberately mismatched across weights — the bold is dramatically wider than the regular — so a hero doesn't behave like normal type, and that engineered-but-off quality is why it reads as frontier tech rather than another geometric. DM Sans is aggressively normal underneath, which stops the page becoming a manifesto, and DM Mono (same family, same rhythm) takes token counts and latency readouts.
items.notes: Syne runs 400–800 with no italic; the personality only appears at 700+ and at size — below 24px it just looks like a slightly wrong grotesque. Because its weights change width, never hover-swap or animate Syne's weight: the text will reflow. DM Mono has only 300/400/500.

items.name: Alfa Slab One + Work Sans
items.vibe: 1970s ad poster — fat slabs, warm paper, and no irony whatsoever.
items.pairing: Alfa Slab One is a single-weight ultra-slab straight out of the 1970s advertising lineage — enormous ink, tiny counters, zero subtlety. Work Sans descends from early-1900s American grotesques, so it sits in an adjacent historical register: the body copy feels period-correct rather than modern, but it was optimised for screen text, so it actually reads. Same era, opposite volume.
items.notes: Alfa Slab One is 400-only with no italic — nothing to fall back to, so it is display-only and never below 28px; its counters fill in fast. Work Sans is variable 100–900 with italics. Resist making the body face retro too — two period fonts is a costume, not a design.

items.name: Caveat + Lato
items.vibe: A handwritten note in the margin of an otherwise sober document.
items.pairing: This is an accent pairing, not a headline pairing — pretending otherwise is exactly how handwriting fonts ruin sites. Caveat is real handwriting with irregular baselines and connected-feeling strokes; its job is signatures, callouts and margin notes, one line at a time. Lato carries every word that has to be read: a humanist sans with warm, semi-rounded terminals that keeps the friendliness without the affectation.
items.notes: Trap: Lato's weights are 100, 300, 400, 700, 900 — there is no 500 and no 600. Requesting one returns HTTP 400 from Google Fonts and takes the whole stylesheet down with it. Caveat runs 400–700 with no italic; never below 20px, never in all-caps, and never as a real heading a screen-reader user has to navigate by. If more than ~5% of the page is Caveat, the design is broken.

items.name: Roboto Slab + Roboto
items.vibe: Annual-report authority — competent, legible, and completely uninterested in being interesting.
items.pairing: Roboto Slab is Roboto's skeleton with slabs added — identical widths, identical x-height — so headings and body lock to the same grid with no optical adjustment, which is why decks and reports set in this pair never look assembled from parts. The slabs buy just enough gravity for a board audience without importing a second personality that legal review would have opinions about.
items.notes: Roboto Slab has no italic at all — if the house style requires italic headings, this pairing cannot do it. Roboto carries a wdth axis (75–100), useful for dense financial tables. Both are variable 100–900 so the range costs nothing. This is a safe, invisible choice: it will never be the reason anyone remembers the brand.

items.name: Inter Tight + Inter
items.vibe: International Style discipline — one voice, two optical sizes, nothing decorative anywhere.
items.pairing: Swiss typography was never two fonts — it is one face used with discipline, so the correct pairing is a display cut and a text cut of the same design. Inter Tight is Inter with reduced sidebearings and tighter apertures: a 64px headline sets correctly without the manual negative letter-spacing everyone hacks onto Inter, while Inter's text cut keeps 16px body open. Same designer, same skeleton, two optical sizes — that's the reason it looks right.
items.notes: Reach for this the moment you catch yourself writing `letter-spacing: -0.03em` on an Inter headline — Inter Tight already did that properly, at the outline level. Don't use Inter Tight below 24px; the tight fit hurts at text sizes. Inter has an opsz axis (14–32); Inter Tight does not.

items.name: Bricolage Grotesque + Manrope
items.vibe: A hand-set poster on a landing page — deliberately imperfect, extremely loud, very now.
items.pairing: Bricolage Grotesque was drawn against the idea of a neutral grotesque — mismatched details and an opsz axis that reshapes the face as it grows, giving a 72px hero the look of something hand-set rather than defaulted. Manrope beneath it is semi-geometric with a notably even color, so the instant the eye drops out of the hero it stops being entertained and starts reading. All the personality lives in one place, on purpose.
items.notes: Bricolage Grotesque is variable with opsz 12–96 and wdth 75–100 — pin opsz high for heroes (`font-variation-settings: 'opsz' 96`) or it serves text-optimised shapes and the entire reason you picked it evaporates. It has no italic (200–800). Manrope is 200–800 and also has no italic — plan emphasis around weight, not slant.

items.name: Sora + Public Sans
items.vibe: Dense, calm instrumentation — the numbers are the design, the type is just the chrome.
items.pairing: A dashboard's real typographic problem is telling chrome apart from data at a glance. Sora's wider, geometric caps mark section titles as furniture you skip past; Public Sans is narrower with a high x-height, so it fits more label into a table cell without dropping below 13px. Roboto Mono takes every number — its fixed advance width is what stops digits jittering as values refresh, the single most-noticed flaw in a live dashboard.
items.notes: Use Roboto Mono for any value that updates live; for static tables `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on Public Sans is lighter. Sora has no italic (100–800) and is wide — keep it out of table cells or you'll run out of column. Keep the mono at 400/500: bold monospace numbers read as an alert state whether you meant it or not.

items.name: Instrument Serif + Instrument Sans
items.vibe: Restrained premium retail — expensive because of what it leaves out.
items.pairing: Drawn by the same foundry as a matched pair, so proportions and rhythm already agree. The interesting part is the constraint: Instrument Serif has exactly one weight, which forces product-page hierarchy to come from size, space and colour instead of bolding everything — and that restraint is precisely what reads as premium. Instrument Sans supplies the four weights the functional layer (price, variant, cart) actually needs.
items.notes: Instrument Serif ships one weight (400) plus a true italic — there is no bold, so never `font-weight: 600` it; the browser will synthesise a smeared fake. Use it for product names and section titles at 32px+ only. Instrument Sans runs 400–700 with a wdth axis (75–100); the condensed cut earns its keep on long variant names.

items.name: Bitter + Cabin
items.vibe: Plain-spoken and grounded — a report from the field, not a brand campaign.
items.pairing: Bitter is a contemporary slab drawn specifically for screen reading — its slabs give headings a matter-of-fact weight that reads as an organisation which digs wells, where a Didone would read as a bank courting donors. Cabin's humanist skeleton descends from Gill Sans, so it carries genuine warmth through a long impact report without the forced friendliness of a rounded face.
items.notes: Bitter is variable 100–900 with italics; stay at 600/700 for headings — its heaviest weights go blocky. Cabin runs 400–700 with a wdth axis (75–100). Both have modest x-heights, so set body at 17–18px. Be clear-eyed: donation forms live and die on contrast, target size and field count, not on the typeface.

items.name: Lexend + Atkinson Hyperlegible
items.vibe: Designed so the reader never has to work — legibility as the actual brief, not a checkbox.
items.pairing: Atkinson Hyperlegible earns the body slot for one concrete reason: the Braille Institute drew its letterforms to be unmistakable from one another, so I/l/1 and O/0 stop being a guess — which matters far more in body copy than anything aesthetic. Lexend was designed around reducing visual crowding, and its wider, open headings hold that same intent at display size without reintroducing ambiguous shapes.
items.notes: Honest caveat: evidence that any typeface *cures* dyslexia is weak, and "dyslexia fonts" are routinely oversold. The reliable wins are measure (~66ch), line-height ≥1.5, left-aligned never justified text, and real contrast ratios — the font is the smallest lever here. Atkinson Hyperlegible has only 400 and 700 plus italics; there is no 500 or 600, so don't design a medium weight into the system. Lexend has no italic.
